phases.name: Data Audit & Generator Forensics
phases.purpose: Establish what the simulator actually produces before interpreting any downstream signal: schema, missingness, identifiers, split boundaries, class balance and known generator artifacts.
phases.description: The audit resolves 1,852,394 transactions and audits 71 analytical columns. It fingerprints the two source CSVs, checks ten data contracts, establishes the temporal train/test boundary, and records the simulator behaviors that bound every later claim.
key_findings: Train and test are separated by a 48-second boundary, not a random split.
Eleven columns contain structural missingness from first-transaction history.
One data contract is flagged: minimum age is 13.9 years versus an expected ~18.
limitations: Raw CSVs are not present in the workspace; only hashes and derived outputs are available.
The SHA-256 values were recorded as 16-character prefixes, not full digests.

phases.name: Univariate Distributions
phases.purpose: Characterize the marginal distributions of amount, time, category, demographics and geography, and quantify how far fraud separates from genuine activity on each axis.
phases.description: Twenty-four figures cover amount histograms, ECDFs, QQ plots, categorical rates, time profiles and demographic/geographic distributions. The phase establishes the first effect-size estimates rather than relying on p-values.
key_findings: Fraud amounts are shifted far to the right: median $390 versus $47.24 for genuine transactions.
The amount distribution is the strongest univariate separator in the program (KS D = 0.724).
Night hours carry a higher fraud rate than daytime volume would suggest.
limitations: Univariate separation does not establish incremental predictive value.
Amount outliers are retained in the analysis; the maximum is 28,948.90.

phases.name: Bivariate & Interaction Analysis
phases.purpose: Test whether risk concentrates in combinations of category, time, geography and cardholder behavior, and measure the money exposure behind transaction counts.
phases.description: The interaction phase links category × hour, card profiles, city and ZIP3 structure, the fraud-dollar lens, mutual information and association structure. It distinguishes real structure from generator-driven artifacts.
key_findings: shopping_net is the highest-volume high-risk category at 1.59% fraud versus a 0.52% baseline.
Merchant coordinates are jittered per transaction; distance is a simulator artifact, not physical travel.
97.7% of cards experience at least one fraud event—an important simulator boundary, not a production prior.
limitations: Merchant and category are almost redundant; merchant-level effects should not be over-interpreted.
Geographic claims are restricted by the simulator's coordinate model.

phases.name: Temporal Structure
phases.purpose: Determine whether fraud is temporally clustered and how volume, seasonality and structural breaks evolve across the 2019–2020 observation window.
phases.description: Rolling statistics, weekly fraud-rate series, STL decomposition, ACF/PACF, time-profile heatmaps, PELT change-point sensitivity and card timelines are used to separate campaign-like clustering from calendar effects.
key_findings: Daily fraud rate has lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.503, evidence of temporal clustering.
Volume has strong weekly periodicity (lag-7 = 0.869); STL seasonality strength is 0.21.
Two consensus structural breaks are stable across PELT penalties; no holiday proximity was found.
limitations: Two breaks are a small number of events; causal attribution to campaigns is not established.
The observations are simulated; calendar effects are properties of the generator.

phases.name: Advanced Visualization & Dimensionality Reduction
phases.purpose: Test whether fraud separates without labels using embeddings, clustering and anomaly detection, and document the limits of visual separability.
phases.description: PCA, t-SNE and UMAP embeddings are scored with logistic AUC. K-Means, DBSCAN and hierarchical clustering are profiled, alongside Isolation Forest, an autoencoder and LOF. High-dimensional visual encodings are evaluated for honesty.
key_findings: PCA(2) reaches logistic AUC 0.816; nonlinear embeddings do not improve separability.
Anomaly detectors isolate fraud only weakly (AUC 0.731–0.881).
DBSCAN labels 4% of points as noise, with a 6.08% fraud rate in that noise.
limitations: Embedding AUC is a property of a 2D representation, not a deployable classifier.
LOF was evaluated on 5,000 rows versus 50,000 for the other anomaly models; AUCs are not directly comparable.

phases.name: Statistical Testing & Effect Sizes
phases.purpose: Replace significance-only claims with effect sizes, bootstrap intervals, multiple-testing correction and inference that respects the card-level repeated measures.
phases.description: Mann–Whitney tests are paired with Cliff's delta, KS statistics, bootstrap CIs and BH-FDR. Categorical associations use Cramér's V with post-hoc correction, and a card-clustered logistic model shows how naive standard errors mislead.
key_findings: Fraud amounts show Cliff's delta 0.669 [0.656, 0.680] and KS D 0.724 [0.715, 0.732].
Five of eight logit effects survive card-clustered standard errors.
72 of 91 category-pair post-hoc tests remain significant after Bonferroni correction.
limitations: Cramér's V is not comparable across variables with very different cardinality (e.g., ZIP3 with 532 levels).
The logistic model uses a 200,000-row sample and 961 card clusters, not the full 1.85M rows.

phases.name: Feature Engineering & Depth Analyses
phases.purpose: Build leak-aware behavioral features and test whether velocity, cohorts, hazards, hierarchical shrinkage and encoding choices add interpretable signal.
phases.description: This phase constructs expanding, train-only target encodings, prior-transaction statistics and velocity features. It adds cohorts, discrete-time hazard, merchant hierarchical empirical Bayes, repeated-fraud events and an hour-encoding comparison.
key_findings: Night + risky category + amount ≥ $500 reaches a 22.08% fraud rate, 42.4× baseline.
38,005 transactions (2.05%) imply speeds above 1,000 km/h—physically impossible transitions.
No affected card has two distinct fraud events more than 7 days apart; compromises are bursty.
Fraud rate rises monotonically with implied speed and trailing-window counts.
limitations: The high-risk combination is descriptive, not a causal effect.
The simulator gives fraud to nearly every card; cohorts and hazards are not production priors.

phases.name: Model Closure & Evaluation
phases.purpose: Measure leak-free predictive performance, diagnose train→test transfer, calibrate probabilities and translate scores into review-budget economics.
phases.description: A 27-feature LightGBM is evaluated with adversarial validation, per-feature PSI, walk-forward CV and leave-card-out CV. Calibration, cost-sensitive thresholds, capture@k, learning curves, ablation, SHAP, PDP/ICE and segment errors complete the loop.
key_findings: Final model: test PR-AUC 0.5575 [0.5365, 0.5784], ROC-AUC 0.9677.
Walk-forward in-domain PR-AUC is 0.9510 ± 0.0152, but the same folds transfer at 0.4726 ± 0.0761.
Adversarial validation separates train and test at AUC 0.99999994; 7 of 27 features have severe PSI.
Top 1% of test by score captures 65.5% of fraud events and 68.7% of fraud dollars.
Removing card_prior_fraud raises test PR-AUC from 0.5575 to 0.8315, localizing the transfer failure.
limitations: Test metrics measure out-of-distribution transfer, not typical generalization.
No epoch-level training history or hardware telemetry was logged.
The final model's probability calibration is not directly comparable to the temperature-scaling split.

phases.name: Report & Reproducibility
phases.purpose: Compile the graded findings ledger, figure/table index, reproducibility checklist and output bundle, and verify the expected phase-8 artifacts exist.
phases.description: The closing phase writes 64 findings, 129 figure captions and an 11-item reproducibility checklist. It verifies 9/9 expected phase-8 tables and creates a 17.9 MB output bundle (not included in this workspace).
key_findings: 64 findings compiled: 30 strong, 27 supports, 6 caveats and 1 weak.
All 11 reproducibility checklist items are marked true.
The notebook reports 9/9 expected phase-8 tables present.
limitations: The 17.9 MB bundle referenced by the run is not present in the workspace.
The report summary says 45 tables, while 46 CSV tables are present.

issues.title: Raw source datasets are absent from the workspace
issues.summary: Only the notebook, derived tables, figures and logs are present. fraudTrain.csv and fraudTest.csv are referenced by hash and size but are not in the folder.
evidence: logs/data_fingerprint.json records 351.2 MB and 150.4 MB source files.
No CSV or ZIP larger than 1 MB exists under the project root.
issues.impact: The analytical outputs can be inspected but the notebook cannot be rerun end-to-end from this folder alone.
issues.action: Add the Kaggle source files (or an authorized copy) and run the rebuild pipeline with FRAUD_PROJECT_ROOT set.

issues.title: Train→test shift makes every test metric an OOD estimate
issues.summary: Train and test are almost perfectly separable by cumulative-history features. The final model's test PR-AUC is a cross-boundary transfer estimate, not a typical generalization estimate.
evidence: 7 of 27 model features have severe PSI (≥0.25).
Walk-forward PR-AUC 0.9510 ± 0.0152 versus test transfer 0.4726 ± 0.0761 for the same folds.
issues.impact: Quoting 0.5575 as “model accuracy” without the OOD context would overstate production readiness.
issues.action: Report in-domain and cross-boundary metrics side by side; validate on a genuinely external, later cohort before deployment.

issues.title: card_prior_fraud dominates the transfer failure
issues.summary: Removing the causal prior-fraud count raises test PR-AUC from 0.5575 to 0.8315. The feature is causally constructed but its distribution shifts sharply across the split.
evidence: 97.7% of cards already have at least one train-period fraud event in the simulator.
issues.impact: The feature may encode campaign timing / generator mechanics rather than transferable fraud behavior.
issues.action: Retrain without card_prior_fraud and compare on external data; model fraud-label latency explicitly before using prior fraud in real time.

issues.title: Simulator artifacts limit external validity
issues.summary: Several apparently predictive structures are properties of the Sparkov generator: near-universal card fraud, per-transaction merchant coordinate jitter, deterministic-ish merchant categories and impossible travel speeds.
evidence: 97.7% of cards have at least one fraud event.
Median per-merchant latitude standard deviation = 5.10° (~566 km); coordinates are not fixed stores.
Merchant_single_category = False; max categories per merchant = 2.
issues.impact: Distance, merchant and card-history priors should not be transferred to production without revalidation.
issues.action: Re-run the feature and cohort analyses on real transaction data with stable merchant identifiers and label latency.

issues.title: One strong finding is contradicted by its own evidence
issues.summary: The target-encoding leakage demo reports naive ρ=0.048 and causal ρ=0.048, yet its finding says full-data encoding overstates the signal.
evidence: notebook cell 52 output: naive TE corr 0.048, causal TE corr 0.048.
issues.impact: A reader could cite an inflation effect that the recorded numbers do not show.
issues.action: Revise the claim to a null result or supply a stronger leakage metric; keep the causal encoding as a methodological safeguard.

issues.title: Cramér's V comparisons ignore cardinality bias
issues.summary: ZIP3 has 532 levels and V=0.148; category has 14 levels and V=0.067. Raw V is not comparable across these cardinalities.
issues.impact: “Category is the strongest categorical association” is not established by the table.
issues.action: Use bias-corrected Cramér's V or a permutation baseline; rank only within comparable cardinalities.

issues.title: Age contract violation is unresolved
issues.summary: The minimum age is 13.9 years, below the ~18 expected for a cardholder. The record is flagged but not corrected.
issues.impact: Minor for aggregate EDA; potentially material for age-segment analysis or any production-like use.
issues.action: Inspect the source rows and decide whether to exclude, cap or retain with a documented rule.

issues.title: ZIP codes lose leading zeros
issues.summary: 116,389 transactions have ZIP values below 10,000, consistent with leading-zero loss after numeric parsing.
issues.impact: ZIP-level joins and geography analyses may misclassify Northeast ZIPs.
issues.action: Read ZIP as string with zero-padding; re-run ZIP3 aggregation if exact geography matters.

issues.title: Structural missingness reaches 10.79%
issues.summary: Prior-transaction and z-score features are missing for the first transaction on a card; amt_z_prior is missing in 10.79% of rows.
issues.impact: Models and PDP routines must handle NaN explicitly; dropping rows would bias first-transaction behavior.
issues.action: Retain explicit missing indicators and document LightGBM's native NaN handling.

issues.title: The cost-minimizing operating point is precision-costly
issues.summary: At the cost-min threshold (≈0.00001), recall is 84.2% but 20,322 genuine transactions are flagged (precision 8.2%). At a 1% review budget, precision is 25.3% and 4,153 genuine transactions are flagged.
issues.impact: The economically optimal threshold may be operationally infeasible without review capacity.
issues.action: Choose an operating point against measured analyst capacity; report expected false-positive workload alongside recall.

issues.title: Optimal threshold is fragile to the false-positive cost
issues.summary: Across $1–$50 false-positive friction, the optimal threshold moves from 0.0000 to 0.0004 and recall ranges from 91.6% to 70.2%.
issues.impact: A single cost assumption should not be treated as a stable policy.
issues.action: Present a cost-sensitivity range and tie the final threshold to a governance decision.

issues.title: Evidence excerpts are capped at 400 characters
issues.summary: The notebook's log_finding function stores str(evidence)[:400]. The ledger therefore contains excerpts, not full supporting objects.
issues.impact: Some findings cannot be independently reproduced from the ledger alone.
issues.action: Store full structured evidence and stable cell/line references; keep the short excerpt for display.

issues.title: Phase numbering is inconsistent across artifacts
issues.summary: Figure/table prefixes use phase0..phase5, phase7, phase8; the findings ledger uses section-phase 1..8. Phase 6 is absent from artifact names.
evidence: findings_ledger.csv uses phase 1 for the §01 audit.
issues.impact: Naive joins on phase number mis-associate findings and artifacts.
issues.action: This dashboard uses canonical P0–P8 IDs with explicit source-prefix and ledger mappings. The source artifacts remain unchanged.

issues.title: Runtime and resource telemetry is largely absent
issues.summary: Only the end-to-end run window, six embedding timings and one SHAP timing are recorded. There is no per-phase duration, CPU/GPU utilization, VRAM or inference-latency series.
evidence: notebook cell 42: t-SNE 321/352/410 s; UMAP 51/36/20 s.
issues.impact: The performance page cannot attribute cost to phases or hardware.
issues.action: Instrument phase timers, device telemetry and inference latency in the next run.

issues.title: Seven interactive maps have no static preview
issues.summary: Plotly 5.24.1 is incompatible with Kaleido 1.5.0, so static map exports were skipped. The HTML artifacts were retained and are included in this gallery.
evidence: notebook cell 4: UserWarning about Plotly/Kaleido versions.
‘kaleido PNG skipped’ appears for 7 map/3D artifacts.

issues.title: Output bundle and full provenance digests are missing

auditNotes.title: The leakage-demo claim is not supported by its own numbers
auditNotes.claim: The ledger says every pipeline using full-data target encoding overstates its signal.
auditNotes.observation: The recorded Spearman correlations are 0.048 for the naive encoding and 0.048 for the causal encoding—equal at the displayed precision. The notebook output does not demonstrate inflation.
auditNotes.implication: Keep the causal encoding as good practice, but do not use this finding as evidence that naive encoding inflated this dataset's signal.

auditNotes.title: “Bimodal” card fraud is really zero-inflation plus a broad rate distribution
auditNotes.claim: Per-card fraud rate is described as bimodal because 2.3% of cards never see fraud and 97.7% see it at least once.
auditNotes.observation: The 999 card profiles show 23 cards with zero fraud and 976 with one or more events. The positive cards have fraud rates spread from near zero to 100%; that is not a two-peak distribution.
auditNotes.implication: The substantive point—fraud is card-clustered—stands. The word “bimodal” should be replaced with “zero-inflated / near-universal exposure.”

auditNotes.title: Merchant→category is near-deterministic, not strictly deterministic
auditNotes.claim: The ledger calls merchant→category deterministic collinearity.
auditNotes.observation: The generator forensics record merchant_single_category = False and max categories per merchant = 2.
auditNotes.implication: Treat merchant and category as near-redundant representations with a small number of exceptions, not as an exact functional dependency.

auditNotes.title: Cramér's V is compared across very different cardinalities
auditNotes.claim: Category is described as having the strongest categorical association with fraud.
auditNotes.observation: Category V = 0.067 over 14 levels, but ZIP3 V = 0.148 over 532 levels. Uncorrected Cramér's V rises mechanically with cardinality and the table does not apply a bias correction.
auditNotes.implication: Do not rank categorical variables by raw V. Use a bias-corrected statistic or permutation null before declaring a strongest categorical association.

auditNotes.title: Artifact count differs from the notebook's closing summary
auditNotes.observation: The workspace contains 46 CSV tables, including figure_index.csv, findings_ledger.csv and reproducibility_checklist.csv.
auditNotes.implication: Counts should be taken after all closing artifacts are written. The dashboard uses the observed 46.

gradeDefs.label: Strong
gradeDefs.definition: Direct quantitative evidence with uncertainty or an explicit comparison; supports the stated claim.
gradeDefs.interpretation: Researcher-assigned grade in the project ledger. The notebook does not publish a formal rubric; this dashboard treats it as the strongest tier.

gradeDefs.label: Supports
gradeDefs.definition: Quantitative evidence consistent with the claim, but narrower or less direct than a strong finding.
gradeDefs.interpretation: Researcher-assigned grade. May depend on a single figure, table or summary statistic.

gradeDefs.label: Weak
gradeDefs.definition: A fragile or ambiguous signal that should not carry a conclusion on its own.
gradeDefs.interpretation: Only one ledger finding carries this grade: the PELT structural-break interpretation.

gradeDefs.label: Caveat
gradeDefs.definition: A limitation, generator artifact or interpretation boundary rather than a positive claim.
gradeDefs.interpretation: Caveats are used to bound external validity and should travel with the findings they qualify.
